śiśṭas; śiṣṭācāra
------------------------------------------
A śiṣṭa is one who is well-trained in moral and ethical behaviour as described in the śāstras or scriptures. The code of conduct prescribed for him is śiṣṭācāra. It comprises the following virtues: सत्य (truth), तपस् (austerity), दान (giving gifts to the needy), alobha (absence of greed), विद्या (learning), ijyā (performing sacrifices), pūjana (worshipping gods and elders) and दम (self-control).
Other virtues mentioned in the works on धर्म are: absence of jealousy and egoism; freedom from hypocrisy, arrogance, delusion and anger; acquisition of Vedic wisdom as per the norms set by tradition.
Śiṣṭācāra is also a source of धर्म.

śiśnadevas
(‘those who considered the phallus as their deity’)
------------------------------------------
This word occurs in the Ṛgveda twice (7.21.5; 10.99.3). Though its literal meaning refers to people who consider the śiśna (= phallus) as deva (= deity), सायण interprets it as people who are lecherous. They were to be kept out of the cultured and decent society.

Śiśumāra
------------------------------------------
Dhruva, the child prince, secured for himself, the boon of ruling over his ड़थेर्’s kingdom here and also a celestial region after death, by pleasing विष्णु through his austerities and devotion.
This celestial region comprising an assemblage of luminaries as a formation in the shape of शिशुमार (an alligator) is called शिशुमार or Śiśumāracakra. It houses its master ध्रुव in its tail-region. ध्रुव moves the entire region, himself also moving with it.
Viṣṇu or नारायण is the support of the whole system.
Gazing at this formation every night with a specific prayer will free one from all the sins committed during the day. He will also attain a long life (vide Viṣṇupurāṇa 2.9 and 12; Bhāgavata 5.23).

śiṣya
(‘one who is fit to be trained’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism prescribes special qualifications, both for the गुरु (the teacher) and for the शिष्य (the disciple) in every field of knowledge.
One of the most general descriptions prescribes the following as the basic and minimum qualification: peaceful nature, humility, purity of मिन्द्, faith in the गुरु, capacity to absorb and retain the knowledge taught by him, efficiency, birth in a good family, intelligence, good conduct and the ability to repay the debt to the गुरु in some form.
According to other sources, an intense desire to learn, inquisitive nature and service to the गुरु are other qualifications expected in a शिष्य.
See GURU also.

Śiśupāla
------------------------------------------
One of the villains depicted in the Mahābhārata, शिशुपाल was the son of Damaghoṣa (the king of Cedi) and Śruta-śravā (sister of कुन्ती). He was born with four hands and three eyes. A voice from the void declared that he, in whose lap the child will lose its extra limbs, will ultimately be its killer. When this happened in कृष्ण’s lap, Śrutaśravā begged कृष्ण to forgive him a hundred times. कृष्ण consented.
When शिशुपाल ascended the throne of the kingdom of Cedi, he proved to be a great tyrant and womaniser.
During the राजसूय sacrifice, he abused कृष्ण right and left. कृष्ण forgave his abuses upto a hundred times and then killed him with his सुदर्शन discus.
He was the third इन्चर्नतिओन् of जय (gatekeeper of वैकुण्ठ) who had been cursed by the four sages (Sanaka and his brothers). हिरण्यकशिपु and रावण were his earlier incarnations.
